error_modes.label: Altitude control during climb out and level off on the departure

texts.0: SP, due to a climb attitude flown by outside reference alone with no altimeter cross-check, did not level the formation off at the altitude assigned for the departure. The aircraft went about 500 feet above the assigned level with the trend still developing while the wingman was struggling to stay in position. IP had to take the controls to recover the assigned altitude and re-stabilize the formation.
texts.1: SP set a climb attitude that was not adjusted as the airspeed built, so the level off was started late and the altitude excursion reached 300 feet, exactly at the limit of the standard. SP corrected only after repeated verbal calls from IP, and the recovery was abrupt enough to force the wingman into a large power reduction. The formation was returned to the assigned altitude but a residual error was carried into the transit.
texts.2: SP began the level off slightly late and the formation climbed about 220 feet above the assigned departure altitude. SP identified the deviation on the altimeter and flew the formation smoothly back to the cleared level with no intervention by IP. The excursion stayed between the 150 and 300 foot bands, but the lead point for the level off should have been anticipated earlier.
texts.3: SP flew the climb and the level off within 100 feet of the assigned departure altitude throughout. Pitch changes were led early enough for the wingman to hold position without large power changes. Every deviation was detected on the altimeter and removed immediately.
texts.4: SP held the departure altitudes within about 40 feet, with each level off anticipated so precisely that the altimeter needle simply stopped on the assigned value. Rates were gentle and predictable, so the formation stayed locked together and nothing more than light control pressure was ever required.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the altitude standard, but the deviations clustered near 140 feet and were consistently high after each level off. The corrections were effective yet started later than required and were larger than the wingman could absorb comfortably. SP is expected to anticipate the level off lead point so that the altitude trace tightens over the next sorties.

texts_at.0: SP flew the departure climb and level off with the lead point for the level-off talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first departure at this stage and the altimeter cross-check against the assigned altitude has not yet become continuous. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to anticipate the level-off lead point without the reminder on the next departures.
texts_at.1: SP held the departure climb and level off with the altitude deviation reaching about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, because the level-off lead point was recognized only as the assigned altitude arrived rather than anticipated in advance. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to pick the level-off lead point earlier so the deviation does not run to the edge of the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP held the departure altitude to roughly 220 feet from the assigned value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the pitch correction at the level off was applied a beat after the trend was visible on the altimeter. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the pitch correction as soon as the trend appears rather than after it has developed.
texts_at.3: SP held the departure altitude within 150 feet on three of the four climb-outs, the fourth needing a slightly larger correction after a level off that was anticipated a little late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to anticipate every level off with the same lead the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP led the departure climb and level off, holding the altitude deviation to about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, once the lead point was anticipated. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP caught the developing altitude trend and flew the formation back to the assigned level with a deviation of about 220 feet, correcting smoothly with no intervention by IP. Anticipating the level-off lead point before the trend is visible, rather than after, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control on the departure climb.
texts_above.3: SP led the pitch changes early enough that the climb and level off stayed within 150 feet of the assigned departure altitude throughout, with every deviation detected on the altimeter and removed immediately. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude control on the departure climb.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated each level off so precisely that the altimeter needle simply stopped on the assigned value, holding the departure altitude within about 40 feet with rates gentle enough that the formation stayed locked together. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude control on the departure climb.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control in the climb and the transit to the flight area

texts.0: SP, due to power left at the climb setting after the level off and no scan of the airspeed indicator, allowed the speed to run about 35 knots above the briefed transit value. The wingman could not hold the briefed position from the outside of the turn and fell behind the formation. IP had to reduce power and reset the transit speed.
texts.1: SP made power changes without reference to the airspeed indicator, so the speed drifted 20 knots off the briefed value, at the limit of the standard. The correction was started only after IP called the deviation twice, and the throttle movement was large enough to displace the wingman from position. The briefed speed was regained late in the transit.
texts.2: SP was slow to reset power after the level off and the airspeed reached about 15 knots above the briefed value. SP detected the deviation, made a small power correction and re-established the briefed transit speed without any intervention by IP. The deviation stayed between the 10 and 20 knot bands, but the power reset should have been made together with the level off.
texts.3: SP maintained the climb and transit speeds within 10 knots of the briefed values. Power was set at each phase change and refined with small corrections, so the wingman held position with modest throttle activity.
texts.4: SP held the briefed airspeeds within about 4 knots for the whole departure and transit, setting power in a single movement at each phase change. The speed was so stable that the wingman flew the transit with almost no throttle correction.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the airspeed standard, but the values sat near 18 knots fast during the transit and were reduced only after the wingman asked for a slower speed. Each correction worked, yet it was reactive rather than planned. SP is expected to set the transit power at the level off so the speed stabilizes without prompting.

texts_at.0: SP flew the climb and transit with the power reset at the level-off talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first departure at this stage and the cross-check between the power setting and the airspeed indicator has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to set the transit power at the level-off without the reminder on the next departures.
texts_at.1: SP held the climb and transit airspeed about 20 knots off the briefed value, at the tolerance limit, because the power reset after the level off was made without reference to the airspeed indicator. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set the transit power at the level off itself so the speed is not left to drift before it is corrected.
texts_at.2: SP let the airspeed reach about 15 knots off the briefed value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the power reset after the level off was made a little later than the phase change required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the power reset together with the level off rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP held the climb and transit airspeed within 10 knots of the briefed value on three of the four departures, the fourth needing a small refinement after a power setting that was a touch conservative. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to set the same power on every departure that produced the first three.

texts_above.1: SP held the climb and transit airspeed to about 20 knots off the briefed value, at the tolerance limit, once the power reset was cross-checked against the airspeed indicator. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP detected the airspeed drifting toward 15 knots off the briefed value and made a small power correction without prompting, re-establishing the transit speed before the deviation grew further. Resetting power together with the level off, rather than afterward, would trim that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound energy management on the climb and transit.
texts_above.3: SP set power at each phase change and refined it with small corrections so the climb and transit speeds stayed within 10 knots of the briefed values throughout, with the wingman needing only modest throttle activity. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed energy management on the climb and transit.
texts_above.4: SP applied power ahead of every pitch change so the whole revised profile was flown with airspeed deviations of only a few knots, and the wingman never needed a large throttle correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional energy management on the climb and transit.

error_modes.label: Accuracy of the assigned departure heading on rollout

texts.0: SP, due to a rollout flown by outside reference without checking the heading indicator, steadied the formation about 18 degrees off the departure heading assigned by ATC. The error was not recognized and the formation continued to diverge from the published departure track. IP had to take over to regain the assigned heading before the airspace boundary.
texts.1: SP rolled out of the departure turn 10 degrees off the assigned heading, exactly at the limit of the standard. The correction was made only after IP pointed out the error, and the second turn was large enough to force the wingman to correct with bank and power. The assigned heading was regained late.
texts.2: SP anticipated the rollout late and steadied about 8 degrees off the assigned departure heading. SP checked the heading indicator, corrected with a shallow turn that the wingman could easily follow and settled on the assigned heading with no intervention by IP. The error stayed between the 5 and 10 degree bands, but the lead into the rollout should have been taken earlier.
texts.3: SP rolled out on the assigned departure headings within 5 degrees on every turn. The lead into the rollout matched the bank used, and the heading indicator was checked to confirm the value rather than assumed.
texts.4: SP steadied on each assigned heading within about 2 degrees, with the rollout anticipated so that no secondary correction was needed. The formation tracked the published departure route with no visible wander.
texts.marginal: SP held the heading standard, but the rollouts settled near 9 degrees off and were tidied up only after a second look at the heading indicator. The final values were acceptable while the technique remained a two stage correction. SP is expected to lead the rollout by the correct amount so that the first rollout is the final one.

texts_at.0: SP rolled out of the departure turn with the heading indicator check talked through by the IP before the roll-out was accepted, because this is SP's first departure at this stage and anticipating the roll-out point has not yet become automatic. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to anticipate the roll-out and check the heading indicator without the reminder on the next departures.
texts_at.1: SP rolled out about 10 degrees off the assigned departure heading, at the tolerance limit, because the roll out was started after the planned heading had already begun to pass. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to anticipate the roll out earlier so the heading is captured without a second turn.
texts_at.2: SP exited the turn about 7 degrees from the planned heading, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the anticipation of the roll out came a little late while the next maneuver was being selected. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fix the roll out point before the turn begins rather than adjusting it during the turn.
texts_at.3: SP exited every turn within 5 degrees of the planned heading on three of the four departures, the fourth needing a small correction after a roll out anticipated a fraction late. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to anticipate the fourth roll out as precisely as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP rolled out about 10 degrees off the assigned departure heading, at the tolerance limit, once the heading indicator was checked to confirm the value. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a roll out drifting toward 7 degrees off the planned heading and corrected it with a shallow, predictable turn that the wingman could follow easily, without any prompting. Anticipating the roll out earlier, rather than correcting it afterward, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid roll-out precision on the departure turns.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated the roll out on every turn of the adapted profile so the exit heading stayed within 5 degrees of the planned value, with the wingman able to hold position without any additional correcting turn. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate roll-out precision on the departure turns.
texts_above.4: SP established the exit heading of each maneuver on the planned value with a negligible error and without any secondary correction, so the axis of the profile remained exactly as planned. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary roll-out precision on the departure turns.

error_modes.label: Leading the formation at a rate the wingman can hold

texts.0: SP, due to bank and power changes made without regard to the wingman's position, applied a rollout and a large power reduction together that the wingman could not match. The wingman was left well outside the briefed position with an overtake that could not be controlled and formation integrity was lost. IP had to direct a rejoin and take over the maneuvering.
texts.1: SP used abrupt control inputs during the departure turns and the wingman was displaced from the briefed position on each one. SP moderated the inputs only after IP called for smoother leading, and the wingman remained unstable for most of the climb. The formation stayed together only through the wingman's own corrections.
texts.2: SP started the departure turns with more bank than briefed, so the wingman went momentarily wide. SP recognized the effect, reduced the bank and flew the remaining turns at a rate the wingman could hold, with no intervention by IP. Formation safety was never in doubt, but the first input should have been sized for the wingman.
texts.3: SP led the formation with smooth and predictable inputs throughout the departure. Bank, pitch and power changes were made at a rate the wingman could match, and the briefed position was held through every turn and the level off.
texts.4: SP flew the whole departure as if from the wingman's cockpit, starting every input gently and holding it steady until completion. The wingman remained locked in the briefed position with no visible correction and the formation moved as a single aircraft.
texts.marginal: SP kept the formation safe and together, but the inputs were sized for the leader rather than for the wingman, who was working hard to hold position. No intervention was necessary and the standard was met. SP is expected to smooth the entry and the exit of each turn so the wingman can hold position with minimal effort.

texts_at.0: SP led the departure turns with the size of each control input talked through by the IP before it was flown, because this is SP's first departure at this stage and judging an input size the wingman can match has not yet been built. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to size the first input of each turn for the wingman without the reminder on the next departures.
texts_at.1: SP flew the departure turns with control inputs a size larger than the wingman could match without difficulty, correcting only once IP asked for smoother leading, and the wingman remained displaced from the briefed position for most of the climb. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the first input of each turn for the wingman rather than for the leader alone.
texts_at.2: SP started one departure turn with more bank than the wingman could comfortably match, sending the wingman momentarily wide before the bank was reduced and the remaining turns were flown at a rate the wingman could hold. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the first input the same way for every turn rather than only after the wingman goes wide.
texts_at.3: SP led the formation with inputs the wingman could match on three of the four departure turns, the fourth needing a small correction after a bank change that started a touch firmer than the rest of the maneuver. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make the first input of every turn as measured as the other three.

texts_above.1: SP flew the departure turns with control inputs sized for the wingman to match, correcting the rate once smoother leading was called for. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a departure turn started with more bank than the wingman could comfortably follow and eased it back without prompting, so the wingman was only momentarily wide before regaining position. Sizing the first input for the wingman from the start, rather than easing it back afterward, would remove that moment altogether. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady lead technique for the wingman's rate.
texts_above.3: SP led the formation with smooth and predictable inputs throughout the departure, matching bank, pitch and power changes to a rate the wingman could hold through every turn and the level off. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good lead technique for the wingman's rate.
texts_above.4: SP flew the whole departure as if from the wingman's cockpit, starting every input gently and holding it steady until completion, so the wingman remained locked in the briefed position with no visible correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless lead technique for the wingman's rate.

error_modes.label: Clearing and traffic deconfliction while leaving the pattern

texts.0: SP, due to attention held inside the cockpit on the departure instruments with no cross-check of the outside picture, did not clear the airspace ahead and into the turns during the climb out of the pattern. Traffic in the air traffic pattern was never seen and the formation was turned across its track. IP had to take control and maneuver the formation clear.
texts.1: SP performed only a cursory lookout before each departure turn and did not clear the airspace into which the formation was turning. The conflicting aircraft was acquired only after IP called it out twice and the avoiding action was late. Separation was preserved, but the clearing remained reactive for the whole departure.
texts.2: SP was slow in clearing the airspace into the first departure turn and acquired the pattern traffic later than it should have been seen. SP then re-established a proper lookout, called the traffic to the wingman and kept it visually acquired for the rest of the climb without any intervention by IP.
texts.3: SP cleared the airspace before and during every departure turn and kept the pattern traffic visually acquired. Attention was divided correctly between the outside lookout, the wingman and the departure instruments.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous and disciplined lookout throughout the departure, acquiring each conflicting aircraft well before it became a factor and calling it to the wingman. The instrument cross-check was interleaved with the lookout with no loss on either side.
texts.marginal: SP cleared the airspace adequately, but the scan was weighted toward the instruments and the pattern traffic was acquired later than comfortable on two occasions. Separation was never in question and no prompting was required. SP is expected to lead the lookout into each turn so that traffic is seen before it becomes a factor.

texts_at.0: SP cleared the airspace for the departure turns with the lookout sequence talked through by the IP before each turn, because this is SP's first departure at this stage and dividing the scan between the lookout, the wingman and the departure instruments has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to clear into each turn deliberately without the reminder on the next departures.
texts_at.1: SP acquired the pattern traffic only after IP called it out twice, having cleared the airspace into the departure turn only cursorily. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to clear into each turn deliberately, before the bank goes in, rather than relying on a cursory look.
texts_at.2: SP was slow clearing the airspace into the first departure turn and acquired the pattern traffic later than it should have been seen, then re-established a proper lookout and kept the traffic visually acquired for the rest of the climb. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to clear the first turn as thoroughly as the ones that followed it.
texts_at.3: SP cleared the airspace before and during three of the four departure turns without delay, with the pattern traffic on the fourth acquired a moment later than ideal while attention was divided with the wingman. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the same lookout priority on every turn that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP acquired the pattern traffic and cleared the airspace into the departure turn before continuing the climb. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP was slow clearing into the first departure turn but re-established a proper lookout without prompting, acquiring the pattern traffic and calling it to the wingman for the rest of the climb. Clearing the first turn as thoroughly as the later ones, rather than catching up afterward, would remove that lapse. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable lookout discipline on the departure climb.
texts_above.3: SP cleared the airspace before and during every departure turn and kept the pattern traffic visually acquired, dividing attention correctly between the outside lookout, the wingman and the departure instruments. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise lookout discipline on the departure climb.
texts_above.4: SP maintained a continuous and disciplined lookout throughout the departure, acquiring each conflicting aircraft well before it became a factor and interleaving the instrument cross-check with the lookout with no loss on either side. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior lookout discipline on the departure climb.

error_modes.label: Compliance with the local departure procedure out of the traffic pattern

texts.0: SP, due to a departure procedure that had not been studied before the sortie, did not fly the published route out of the air traffic pattern. The formation was turned on course before the departure point and climbed through the pattern altitude inside the traffic circuit, contrary to the Local Area Procedures. IP had to intervene and re-establish the formation on the published departure.
texts.1: SP flew the correct departure route but arrived at the turning point without having reached the climb profile required by the Local Area Procedures. The sequence was corrected only after IP prompted for the published profile and the formation rejoined the procedure late. Nothing further was omitted after the prompt.
texts.2: SP began the departure turn slightly before the published point and the formation was momentarily off the local departure track. SP recognized the error against the visual references, regained the published route and flew the remainder of the procedure as written with no intervention by IP.
texts.3: SP flew the local departure procedure as published, with the pattern exit, the climb profile and the turn on course in the correct sequence. The procedural requirements were applied without prompting and the formation stayed on the published track.
texts.4: SP flew the local departure exactly as published and anticipated every step, so the pattern exit, the climb and the turn on course flowed without a single correction. Departures from the published track were not measurable and the wingman had no extra work to do.
texts.marginal: SP complied with the local departure procedure, but the turn points were identified late and the profile altitudes were reached at the last moment. Nothing was omitted and no prompting was required. SP is expected to fix the sequence of the procedure before the sortie so that the departure steps are anticipated rather than recognized.

texts_at.0: SP flew the local departure procedure with each step of the sequence, from the pattern exit to the turn on course, talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first departure at this stage and the sequence of the Local Area Procedures has not yet been fixed in memory. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to fix the sequence of the procedure without the reminder on the next departures.
texts_at.1: SP flew the correct departure route but arrived at the turning point without having reached the climb profile the Local Area Procedures required, rejoining the procedure only after IP prompted for it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to fix the climb profile against the LAP before the turning point rather than catching up to it after.
texts_at.2: SP began the departure turn slightly before the published point, momentarily off the local departure track, then recognized the error against the visual references and regained the published route without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to identify the published turn point before reaching it rather than during the turn.
texts_at.3: SP flew the local departure procedure as published on three of the four departures, with the fourth showing the turn points identified a moment later than ideal though nothing in the sequence was omitted. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to identify the turn points on every departure with the same margin the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP flew the correct departure route and reached the climb profile the Local Area Procedures required, rejoining the sequence once prompted. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a departure turn started slightly before the published point and regained the local departure track without prompting, flying the remainder of the procedure exactly as written. Identifying the published turn point before starting the turn, rather than during it, would remove that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured procedural discipline on the departure.
texts_above.3: SP flew the local departure procedure as published, with the pattern exit, the climb profile and the turn on course in the correct sequence, applied without prompting and with the formation staying on the published track. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined procedural discipline on the departure.
texts_above.4: SP flew the local departure exactly as published and anticipated every step, so the pattern exit, the climb and the turn on course flowed without a single correction and left the wingman no extra work. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate procedural discipline on the departure.

error_modes.label: Orientation and transit to the assigned flight area

texts.0: SP, due to a loss of situational awareness after the departure turn, did not identify the boundaries of the assigned flight area and led the formation past them. The position relative to the area and to the adjacent airspace was not maintained and SP could not state where the formation was when asked. IP had to take over the navigation and return the formation into the assigned area.
texts.1: SP lost track of the position relative to the assigned flight area during the transit and was heading toward the wrong sector. Orientation was restored only after IP gave the visual references twice, and entry into the area was delayed. The formation stayed clear of the adjacent airspace only because of the prompting.
texts.2: SP misidentified a ground reference during the transit and drifted toward the edge of the assigned area. SP rebuilt the position picture from heading, time and known landmarks, corrected the track and entered the assigned area correctly with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP kept the formation oriented throughout the transit and entered the assigned flight area on the briefed track and at the briefed altitude. Position was cross-checked continuously against ground references and the heading indicator.
texts.4: SP was oriented at every moment of the transit, able to state position, distance and time to the area boundary without hesitation. Entry into the assigned area was made exactly on the briefed track, altitude and timing, with the working area identified before arrival.
texts.marginal: SP maintained orientation and entered the assigned area correctly, but the position picture was rebuilt from landmarks rather than carried continuously and one reference was confirmed late. The result met the standard with no prompting from IP. SP is expected to keep a running position estimate so that the area boundary is anticipated rather than searched for.

texts_at.0: SP flew the transit to the assigned flight area with the ground references and the position picture talked through by the IP along the way, because this is SP's first transit to this area and the running position estimate has not yet been built. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to cross-check position against the planned track without the reminder on the next transits.
texts_at.1: SP lost track of the position relative to the assigned flight area during the transit and was heading toward the wrong sector until IP gave the visual references twice. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cross-check position against the planned track continuously rather than only when it is questioned.
texts_at.2: SP misidentified a ground reference during the transit and drifted toward the edge of the assigned area, then rebuilt the position picture from heading, time and known landmarks and corrected the track without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm each ground reference against more than one cue before using it to correct the track.
texts_at.3: SP kept the formation oriented and entered the assigned flight area on the briefed track on three of the four transits, the fourth needing one ground reference confirmed a little later than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to confirm every reference with the same promptness the first three transits showed.

texts_above.1: SP regained the position relative to the assigned flight area with the visual references given by the IP, then continued the transit toward the correct sector. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP misidentified a ground reference during the transit but rebuilt the position picture from heading, time and known landmarks without prompting, correcting the track and entering the assigned area correctly. Confirming each reference against more than one cue before using it, rather than after a drift develops, would remove that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent navigational awareness on the transit.
texts_above.3: SP kept the formation oriented throughout the transit and entered the assigned flight area on the briefed track and altitude, cross-checking position continuously against ground references and the heading indicator. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed navigational awareness on the transit.
texts_above.4: SP was oriented at every moment of the transit, able to state position, distance and time to the area boundary without hesitation, and entered the assigned area exactly on the briefed track, altitude and timing. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding navigational awareness on the transit.

error_modes.label: Radio calls and visual signals with the wingman and ATC

texts.0: SP, due to a lack of communication with the wingman during the departure, changed power and heading without any radio call or visual signal. The wingman had no notice of the changes and fell out of the briefed position, and one ATC clearance accepted for the formation was never passed on. IP had to make the calls and re-establish the coordination between the two cockpits.
texts.1: SP used non-standard phraseology and passed the changes to the wingman late, so the formation reacted a step behind each ATC instruction. The calls were corrected only after IP prompted for the standard format, and one visual signal had to be repeated before the wingman acknowledged it. The departure was completed with the formation intact.
texts.2: SP passed one clearance change to the wingman later than briefed, so the wingman had to correct to stay in position. SP recognized the omission, returned to the briefed calls and visual signals and kept the wingman informed for the rest of the departure with no intervention by IP.
texts.3: SP passed every ATC clearance and configuration change to the wingman with standard phraseology and the briefed visual signals. Radio work with ATC was concise and correct and the wingman was never left guessing.
texts.4: SP kept the wingman fully informed throughout the departure, giving each change with the correct signal or call before it was flown. Radio work with ATC was accurate and economical and the whole departure was completed without a single request for a repeat.
texts.marginal: SP communicated all the required items, but several calls were made while the change was being flown rather than before it, and the phraseology drifted from the standard on two transmissions. The wingman kept position and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to make the call first and fly the change second so that the wingman has time to respond.

texts_at.0: SP passed the ATC clearances and configuration changes to the wingman with the standard phraseology and the visual signals talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first departure at this stage and passing every change to the wingman before it is flown has not yet become a habit. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to pass every change to the wingman before it is flown without the reminder on the next departures.
texts_at.1: SP passed the changes to the wingman a step behind each ATC instruction, using non-standard phraseology that was corrected only after IP prompted for the standard format. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to pass every change to the wingman before it is flown, in standard phraseology, rather than a step behind it.
texts_at.2: SP passed one clearance change to the wingman later than briefed, so the wingman had to correct to stay in position, then recognized the omission and returned to the briefed calls and visual signals for the rest of the departure without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to pass every clearance change as promptly as the one that was recognized late here.
texts_at.3: SP passed every ATC clearance and configuration change to the wingman with standard phraseology on three of the four departures, the fourth call arriving a moment after the change had already begun to be flown. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to pass that one call with the same lead time the other three showed.

texts_above.1: SP passed the changes to the wingman in standard phraseology once the format was corrected, keeping the formation a step ahead of each ATC instruction from that point on. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a clearance change passed to the wingman later than briefed and returned to the briefed calls and visual signals without prompting, keeping the wingman informed for the rest of the departure. Passing every change before it is flown, rather than catching up after one is missed, would remove that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good coordination with the wingman on the departure.
texts_above.3: SP passed every ATC clearance and configuration change to the wingman with standard phraseology and the briefed visual signals, keeping radio work with ATC concise and correct so the wingman was never left guessing. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good coordination with the wingman on the departure.
texts_above.4: SP kept the wingman fully informed throughout the departure, giving each change with the correct signal or call before it was flown and completing the whole departure without a single request for a repeat. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent coordination with the wingman on the departure.

error_modes.label: Power and airspeed stabilization after the interval takeoff

texts.0: SP, due to leaving MAX power set after becoming airborne instead of reducing to 85 percent at 160 knots, let the departure speed run about 30 knots above the briefed value. The wingman, who started the takeoff roll 10 seconds later, could not generate the closure the rejoin needed and fell further behind along the departure route. IP had to reduce power and reset the rejoin airspeed.
texts.1: SP delayed the reduction to 85 percent well past the 160 knot point and the speed settled 20 knots fast, at the limit of the standard. The power came back only after IP called the airspeed twice, and the wingman had to hold MAX power far longer than planned to close. The briefed departure speed was re-established late in the climb.
texts.2: SP set the power by feel rather than to the briefed 85 percent and the departure speed reached about 15 knots fast. SP checked the airspeed indicator, refined the setting and stabilized on the briefed value with no intervention by IP, so the wingman's overtake stayed workable. The deviation sat between the two bands, but the setting should have been made at the level off from the takeoff.
texts.3: SP reduced power to 85 percent as the aircraft accelerated through 160 knots and held the departure speed within 10 knots of the briefed value. The wingman closed with a normal overtake and no airspeed information had to be passed.
texts.4: SP made a single smooth reduction to 85 percent as the airspeed passed 160 knots and held the departure speed within about 3 knots for the whole climb out. The wingman built a textbook overtake and arrived in route with almost no throttle work.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside the airspeed standard, but the reduction to 85 percent came several seconds after 160 knots and left the speed around 17 knots fast until the first turn. Nothing was needed from IP and the wingman still closed, although with more power than planned. SP is expected to make the reduction as the airspeed passes 160 knots so the platform is stable before the rejoin begins.

texts_at.0: SP reduced power after the interval takeoff with the airspeed reference point for the reduction talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first interval departure at this stage and the timing of the power reduction against the airspeed has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to make the power reduction as the airspeed passes the briefed point without the reminder on the next interval departures.
texts_at.1: SP delayed the reduction to 85 percent until the departure speed settled about 20 knots fast, at the tolerance limit, before the power came back on IP's call. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to make the power reduction as the airspeed passes 160 knots so the departure speed does not need to be recovered afterward.
texts_at.2: SP set the power by feel rather than to the briefed 85 percent and let the departure speed reach about 15 knots fast, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before checking the airspeed indicator and refining the setting without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the 85 percent reduction at the level off itself rather than adjusting it once the speed has already run fast.
texts_at.3: SP held the departure speed within 10 knots of the briefed value on three of the four climb-outs, the fourth needing a small refinement after a power reduction to 85 percent made a moment later than the airspeed called for. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to time the reduction on every departure as precisely as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP delayed the reduction to 85 percent, holding the departure speed to about 20 knots fast, at the tolerance limit, before the power was brought back. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP set power by feel rather than to the briefed 85 percent but caught the resulting 15-knot excess on the airspeed indicator and refined the setting without prompting, keeping the wingman's overtake workable. Making the 85 percent reduction at the level off itself, rather than refining it afterward, would trim that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound power management after the interval takeoff.
texts_above.3: SP reduced power to 85 percent as the aircraft accelerated through 160 knots and held the departure speed within 10 knots of the briefed value, so the wingman closed with a normal overtake and needed no airspeed information. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed power management after the interval takeoff.
texts_above.4: SP made a single smooth reduction to 85 percent as the airspeed passed 160 knots and held the departure speed within about 3 knots for the whole climb out, so the wingman built a textbook overtake with almost no throttle work. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional power management after the interval takeoff.

error_modes.label: Holding a stable platform for the straight ahead rejoin

texts.0: SP, due to continuing to work pitch and power after directing a straight ahead rejoin instead of freezing a stable platform, let the profile wander more than 400 feet. The wingman, closing from the low 6 o'clock with the briefed overtake, lost the established vector and had to break off the rejoin. IP steadied the aircraft and re-established the platform.
texts.1: SP treated the rejoin as ordinary climb flying and kept chasing the altimeter, so the platform moved about 300 feet, at the limit of the standard. The corrections stopped only after IP called for a steady platform, and the wingman had to make the rejoin bid against a moving reference. The rejoin was completed well behind the planned point.
texts.2: SP made an unnecessary pitch correction after directing the rejoin and the platform drifted about 200 feet before it was recognized. SP stopped correcting, held attitude and power steady, and the wingman completed the bid towards the wingtip position without any intervention by IP. The deviation stayed between the two bands, but the platform should have been frozen the moment the rejoin was directed.
texts.3: SP established a stable platform as the rejoin was directed and held the profile within 100 feet with attitude and power unchanged. The wingman closed from behind and slightly below and arrived in route with the same airspeed as the leader.
texts.4: SP froze the platform on the first attitude and power setting and the profile stayed within about 40 feet for the whole rejoin. The wingman flew his closure and his bid against a completely stationary reference and stabilized in route without a correction from the leader.
texts.marginal: SP kept the platform inside the standard, but small pitch corrections continued through the rejoin and the profile moved close to 140 feet each way. The wingman still closed and stabilized and IP said nothing. SP is expected to set the platform once when the rejoin is directed and then leave it alone until the wingman is stabilized in route.

texts_at.0: SP flew the straight ahead rejoin with the platform freeze talked through by the IP as the rejoin was directed, because this is SP's first rejoin at this stage and the habit of freezing attitude and power the moment the rejoin is directed has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to freeze the platform the moment the rejoin is directed without the reminder on the next rejoins.
texts_at.1: SP let the rejoin platform move about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, chasing the altimeter rather than freezing attitude and power once the rejoin was directed, until IP called for a steady platform. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to freeze the platform the moment the rejoin is directed instead of continuing to work pitch and power.
texts_at.2: SP made an unnecessary pitch correction after directing the rejoin and let the platform drift about 200 feet before recognizing it, then held attitude and power steady without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to freeze the platform on the first setting rather than adjusting it once more before holding it steady.
texts_at.3: SP held the rejoin profile within 100 feet on three of the four straight ahead rejoins, the fourth showing a small drift before attitude and power were held steady. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to freeze the platform on the first setting on every rejoin, as the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP froze attitude and power for the rejoin, holding the platform to about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, once the freeze was called for. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP made an unnecessary pitch correction after directing the rejoin but recognized the resulting 200-foot drift without prompting, stopping the correction and holding attitude and power steady for the wingman's bid. Freezing the platform on the first setting, rather than correcting it once more, would remove that drift altogether. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady platform discipline for the straight ahead rejoin.
texts_above.3: SP established a stable platform as the rejoin was directed and held the profile within 100 feet with attitude and power unchanged, so the wingman closed and arrived in route at the same airspeed as the leader. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed platform discipline for the straight ahead rejoin.
texts_above.4: SP froze the platform on the first attitude and power setting and held the profile within about 40 feet for the whole rejoin, so the wingman flew the closure and the bid against a completely stationary reference. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding platform discipline for the straight ahead rejoin.

error_modes.label: Rejoin airspeed and the call when it differs from the briefed value

texts.0: SP, having briefed the standard 180 knot rejoin, flew the departure turn about 25 knots away from that value and never called the actual airspeed. The wingman set closure against the briefed number, arrived with excessive overtake and had to fly out to the outside of the turn. IP called the airspeed and directed the correction.
texts.1: SP allowed the rejoin airspeed to sit 20 knots away from the briefed value and passed the actual figure only after IP asked for it. Because the wingman was working against the wrong reference, the overtake was uncontrolled through the last few hundred feet. The airspeed was reset late and the rejoin needed a second attempt.
texts.2: SP let the rejoin airspeed drift about 15 knots from the briefed value, past the 10 knot difference at which the call is required. SP recognized it, transmitted the actual airspeed and returned to the briefed value with a small power change, so the wingman could reset closure with no intervention by IP.
texts.3: SP held the rejoin airspeed within 10 knots of the briefed value throughout the turn, so no callout was required. The wingman's overtake matched the plan and he stabilized in route approximately co-airspeed.
texts.4: SP flew the rejoin within about 3 knots of the briefed value from roll in to route position. The wingman needed no airspeed information at all and moved into close on the first pass.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the airspeed standard, but the rejoin was flown around 17 knots off the briefed value and the required call came only when the wingman was already inside 500 feet. Nothing was needed from IP and the wingman absorbed the extra overtake. SP is expected to hold the briefed rejoin airspeed and to call any difference of more than 10 knots before the wingman commits to his closure.

texts_at.0: SP flew the turning rejoin with the airspeed call to the wingman talked through by the IP whenever the value moved away from the briefed figure, because this is SP's first rejoin at this stage and calling out the airspeed difference without a prompt has not yet become automatic. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to call any airspeed difference from the briefed value without the reminder on the next rejoins.
texts_at.1: SP let the rejoin airspeed sit about 20 knots away from the briefed value, at the tolerance limit, and passed the actual figure only after IP asked for it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to call any airspeed difference past 10 knots before the wingman commits to the closure, without waiting to be asked.
texts_at.2: SP let the rejoin airspeed drift about 15 knots from the briefed value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before recognizing it, transmitting the actual airspeed and returning to the briefed value with a small power change, all without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the call as soon as the 10-knot difference is reached rather than after it has grown further.
texts_at.3: SP held the rejoin airspeed within 10 knots of the briefed value on three of the four turns, needing no callout, with the fourth drifting a little further before a call was made and the value corrected. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the airspeed within the same margin on every rejoin that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP let the rejoin airspeed sit about 20 knots away from the briefed value, at the tolerance limit, before the actual figure was passed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP let the rejoin airspeed drift to about 15 knots off the briefed value but recognized it, transmitted the actual airspeed and returned to the briefed value with a small power change, all without prompting. Holding the airspeed inside 10 knots from the start, rather than correcting it once the call is made, would remove that transmission. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured airspeed discipline on the rejoin.
texts_above.3: SP held the rejoin airspeed within 10 knots of the briefed value throughout the turn, so no callout was required and the wingman's overtake matched the plan and stabilized approximately co-airspeed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate airspeed discipline on the rejoin.
texts_above.4: SP flew the rejoin within about 3 knots of the briefed value from roll in to route position, so the wingman needed no airspeed information at all and moved into close on the first pass. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary airspeed discipline on the rejoin.

error_modes.label: Bank angle discipline during the turning rejoin on the departure

texts.0: SP varied the bank between shallow and steep instead of holding the briefed 30 degrees, so the aspect the wingman was flying changed continuously. The wingman was driven into a high aspect picture that could not be managed and closed with the vertical stabilizer running out towards the wingtip. IP directed a knock it off and re-established the rejoin turn.
texts.1: SP held the bank only loosely and let it swing well past the briefed 30 degrees on every correction, so the wingman had to work aspect for the whole rejoin. The turn was steadied only after IP called for a constant bank, and the wingman arrived in route with more overtake than planned. The formation stayed together but the reference line was never stable.
texts.2: SP rolled into the rejoin turn with more than the briefed bank and the wingman's aspect built faster than expected. SP saw the vertical stabilizer moving out along the wing, returned to 30 degrees and held it, so the wingman regained the reference line without any intervention by IP.
texts.3: SP established the rejoin turn in level flight at the briefed 30 degrees and held the bank constant until the wingman was stabilized in route. The aspect reference stayed steady and the wingman had no line of sight to work against.
texts.4: SP rolled to the briefed bank in one movement and held it within a couple of degrees for the entire rejoin. The wingman flew a single aspect picture from roll in to route and moved into close without a bank correction of his own.
texts.marginal: SP kept the rejoin turn within the briefed parameters, but the bank drifted a few degrees either side of 30 for most of the turn and the wingman was adjusting aspect continuously. The rejoin was completed safely and IP said nothing. SP is expected to set the bank once and hold it so the wingman flies one aspect picture all the way to route.

texts_at.0: SP flew the turning rejoin with the briefed bank reference talked through by the IP as the turn was established, because this is SP's first rejoin at this stage and holding a constant bank through the whole rejoin has not yet formed. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to set the briefed bank angle once and hold it without the reminder on the next rejoins.
texts_at.1: SP let the rejoin bank swing about 10 degrees wide of the briefed 30, at the tolerance limit, before IP called for a constant bank, so the wingman worked aspect for most of the rejoin. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set the bank once at 30 degrees and hold it rather than letting it swing before a call is needed.
texts_at.2: SP rolled into the rejoin turn with the bank running about 7 degrees past the briefed 30, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before seeing the vertical stabilizer moving out along the wing and returning to 30 degrees without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the bank at 30 degrees on the first input rather than correcting it once the wingman's aspect has already started to build.
texts_at.3: SP held the rejoin bank within 5 degrees of the briefed 30 on three of the four turns, the fourth drifting a touch wider before the wingman's aspect line was fully steady. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same bank precision on every rejoin turn that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP let the rejoin bank swing about 10 degrees wide of the briefed value, at the tolerance limit, before it was set back on the briefed reference. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP rolled into the rejoin turn with the bank running past the briefed 30 by about 7 degrees but saw the vertical stabilizer moving out along the wing and returned to 30 degrees without prompting, so the wingman regained the reference line. Setting 30 degrees on the first input, rather than correcting it once the aspect has started to build, would trim that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent bank discipline on the turning rejoin.
texts_above.3: SP established the rejoin turn in level flight at the briefed bank angle and held it within 5 degrees until the wingman was stabilized in route, so the aspect reference stayed steady with no line of sight to work against. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good bank discipline on the turning rejoin.
texts_above.4: SP rolled to the briefed bank in one movement and held it within a couple of degrees for the entire rejoin, so the wingman flew a single aspect picture from roll in to route and moved into close without a bank correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior bank discipline on the turning rejoin.

error_modes.label: Delay after the pitchout before establishing the rejoin turn

texts.0: SP started the rejoin turn almost immediately after the pitchout, before the wingman had rolled out in trail. The wingman was left with no trail position to work from, ended up close to abeam with angles that could not be solved and the rejoin geometry was unrecoverable. IP rolled out and set the rejoin up again.
texts.1: SP gave the wingman only a token delay after the pitchout, so the turn was established while the wingman was still rolling out. The wingman had to fly a large lead pursuit correction to find the reference line and did so only after IP called the geometry. The rejoin closed, but the aspect was outside the briefed picture for most of it.
texts.2: SP began the rejoin turn slightly early and the wingman entered it from a wide trail position. SP recognized the geometry, eased the turn until the wingman settled behind, and the rejoin then developed normally with no intervention by IP.
texts.3: SP delayed after the pitchout until the wingman was rolled out in trail, then established the turn in level flight at the briefed bank. The wingman entered with the briefed closure and the aspect built at the expected rate.
texts.4: SP timed the delay so that the turn began the moment the wingman's wings were level in trail. The rejoin developed on the reference line from the start and the wingman flew straight to route without an aspect correction.
texts.marginal: SP allowed enough delay for the rejoin to work, but the turn was established while the wingman was still stabilizing in trail and he began with more aspect than briefed. The rejoin was completed without prompting from IP. SP is expected to wait until the wingman is rolled out in trail before establishing the turn.

texts_at.0: SP flew the rejoin turn after the pitchout with the delay before rolling in talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first rejoin at this stage and judging when the wingman is rolled out in trail has not yet been built. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to hold the delay until the wingman is rolled out in trail without the reminder on the next rejoins.
texts_at.1: SP gave the wingman only a token delay after the pitchout, so the wingman had to fly a large lead pursuit correction to find the reference line, recognized only after IP called the geometry. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold the delay until the wingman is rolled out in trail before starting the turn.
texts_at.2: SP began the rejoin turn slightly early with the wingman entering from a wide trail position, then recognized the geometry, eased the turn until the wingman settled behind and let the rejoin develop normally without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm the wingman is rolled out in trail before starting the turn rather than easing it afterward.
texts_at.3: SP delayed after the pitchout until the wingman was rolled out in trail on three of the four rejoins, the fourth turn started a moment early while the wingman was still settling. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to judge that one delay with the same patience the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP judged the delay after the pitchout against the geometry the IP called out, rolling into the rejoin turn once the wingman was confirmed in trail. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP began the rejoin turn a little early with the wingman entering from a wide trail position but recognized the geometry and eased the turn without prompting until the wingman settled behind. Confirming the wingman is rolled out in trail before starting the turn, rather than easing it afterward, would remove that adjustment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady timing of the rejoin turn after pitchout.
texts_above.3: SP delayed after the pitchout until the wingman was rolled out in trail, then established the turn in level flight at the briefed bank so the wingman entered with the briefed closure and the aspect built at the expected rate. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed timing of the rejoin turn after pitchout.
texts_above.4: SP timed the delay so the turn began the moment the wingman's wings were level in trail, so the rejoin developed on the reference line from the start and the wingman flew straight to route without an aspect correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate timing of the rejoin turn after pitchout.

error_modes.label: Monitoring the wingman's aspect and closure through the rejoin

texts.0: SP directed the rejoin and then turned attention elsewhere, so the wingman's excessive overtake was never recognized. Actual airspeed was not compared with the directed value and no evasive action was ready as the wingman closed through the last few hundred feet. IP called the overtake and maneuvered the aircraft to open the geometry.
texts.1: SP monitored the wingman only intermittently and missed the build up of overtake until the separation had closed to about 500 feet. The prompt to check the closure came from IP and the wingman had to fly an overshoot to the outside. Separation was preserved, but the leader was never in a position to take evasive action.
texts.2: SP lost the wingman during the straight ahead rejoin, where the wingman is difficult to see behind and below, and did not read the closure for several seconds. SP re-acquired the wingman, compared actual airspeed with the directed value and monitored the final stage of the rejoin without any intervention by IP.
texts.3: SP kept the wingman in sight throughout the rejoin, monitored aspect and closure and compared actual airspeed with the directed value. The overtake stayed under control through the critical last few hundred feet and no correction was needed.
texts.4: SP tracked the wingman's aspect and closure continuously, called the picture as it developed and stayed ready to maneuver if the overtake grew. The rejoin was monitored from the direction to the route position and the leader was ahead of every stage of it.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the wingman and the rejoin was safe, but attention went inside to the instruments during the final closure and the overtake was assessed late. Nothing was required from IP. SP is expected to hold the monitoring through the critical last few hundred feet, where the closure has to be judged.

texts_at.0: SP monitored the wingman through the rejoin with the scan for the blind part of the straight-ahead rejoin talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first rejoin at this stage and planning the scan for the position behind and below has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to plan the scan for the blind part of the rejoin without the reminder on the next rejoins.
texts_at.1: SP missed the build up of overtake until the wingman was already close in, the prompt to check the closure coming from IP rather than from SP's own monitoring. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold the monitoring of the wingman continuously through the last stage of the rejoin rather than resuming it only when prompted.
texts_at.2: SP lost the wingman during the straight ahead rejoin, where the wingman is difficult to see behind and below, for several seconds before re-acquiring the wingman and comparing actual airspeed with the directed value without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to plan the scan for the blind part of the straight ahead rejoin rather than losing it and recovering afterward.
texts_at.3: SP kept the wingman in sight and monitored the closure through three of the four rejoins, the fourth needing attention to return from the instruments a moment later than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the same monitoring on every rejoin that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP checked the closure of the wingman once the build-up of overtake was pointed out, holding the monitoring through the last stage of the rejoin from that point on. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP lost the wingman briefly during the straight ahead rejoin, a position that is difficult to see behind and below, but re-acquired the wingman and compared actual airspeed with the directed value without prompting. Planning the scan for that blind portion of the rejoin, rather than losing it and recovering afterward, would remove that gap. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable monitoring of the wingman's closure.
texts_above.3: SP kept the wingman in sight throughout the rejoin, monitoring aspect and closure and comparing actual airspeed with the directed value, so the overtake stayed under control through the critical last few hundred feet with no correction needed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined monitoring of the wingman's closure.
texts_above.4: SP tracked the wingman's aspect and closure continuously, calling the picture as it developed and staying ready to maneuver if the overtake grew, monitoring the rejoin from the direction to the route position. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless monitoring of the wingman's closure.

error_modes.label: Announcing and clearing a change of rejoin type on the departure route

texts.0: SP began a departure turn in the middle of a straight ahead rejoin without informing the wingman and without clearing in the direction of the turn. The wingman, set up for pure airspeed closure from the low 6 o'clock, was turned into and ended in an overshoot that could not be controlled. IP rolled out and directed the rejoin again.
texts.1: SP turned the formation onto the next departure leg during the rejoin and told the wingman only after the bank was in. The wingman had to convert to a turning rejoin with no warning and was late recognizing the overshoot, which was corrected after IP called it. The formation stayed safe but the transition was unmanaged.
texts.2: SP started the turn a moment before the call was made, so the wingman began the transition a couple of seconds behind. SP completed the call, cleared into the turn and eased the bank until the wingman was established, with no intervention by IP.
texts.3: SP informed the wingman before every change of rejoin type, cleared in the direction of the turn and kept the bank inside the wingman's capability. The wingman converted from airspeed closure to a turning rejoin without losing the geometry.
texts.4: SP briefed each transition before it was needed, so the wingman was anticipating the change of rejoin type at every turn point on the departure route. Clearing was completed before each turn and the wingman flew one continuous closure to route position.
texts.marginal: SP kept the wingman informed and the transitions worked, but the calls were made as the bank went in rather than before it and the wingman was always reacting. No prompting from IP was needed. SP is expected to call and clear the turn first and roll second, so the wingman can convert to a turning rejoin without losing his closure.

texts_at.0: SP flew the change of rejoin type with the call-and-clear sequence talked through by the IP before the turn was made, because this is SP's first rejoin transition at this stage and calling the turn before the bank goes in has not yet formed. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to call and clear the turn before the bank goes in without the reminder on the next departures.
texts_at.1: SP turned the formation onto the next departure leg during the rejoin and told the wingman only after the bank was in, so the wingman had to convert to a turning rejoin with no warning and was late recognizing the overshoot until IP called it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to call and clear the turn before the bank goes in rather than during it.
texts_at.2: SP started the turn a moment before the call was made, so the wingman began the transition a couple of seconds behind, then completed the call, cleared into the turn and eased the bank until the wingman was established, all without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the call before the bank goes in rather than a moment after it.
texts_at.3: SP informed the wingman before the change of rejoin type on three of the four transitions, the fourth call made as the bank was already going in rather than just before it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to lead that one call with the same timing the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP called and cleared the turn onto the next departure leg once the overshoot was pointed out, letting the wingman convert to the turning rejoin from that call onward. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP started a turn a moment before the call was made but completed the call, cleared into the turn and eased the bank without prompting until the wingman was established on the new rejoin type. Making the call before the bank goes in, rather than a moment after, would remove that lag. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound coordination of the rejoin transition.
texts_above.3: SP informed the wingman before every change of rejoin type, cleared in the direction of the turn and kept the bank inside the wingman's capability, so the wingman converted from airspeed closure to a turning rejoin without losing the geometry. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good coordination of the rejoin transition.
texts_above.4: SP briefed each transition before it was needed, so the wingman was anticipating the change of rejoin type at every turn point and clearing was completed before each turn, letting the wingman fly one continuous closure to route position. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent coordination of the rejoin transition.

error_modes.label: Choosing the wingman's side from the wind and the turn out of traffic

texts.0: SP selected the side for the wingman without considering the wind or the direction of the turn out of traffic, leaving the wingman on the inside of the first departure turn. The wingman was forced under the leader with no room as the turn began and could not hold a safe position. IP reversed the turn and repositioned the formation.
texts.1: SP placed the wingman on the wrong side for the briefed turn out of traffic and recognized it only after IP pointed it out. The turn had to be flown with reduced bank to keep the wingman clear and the departure heading was reached about 10 degrees off before it was corrected. The formation stayed safe but the geometry worked against the wingman throughout.
texts.2: SP weighed the wind but not the direction of the turn out of traffic when choosing the side, so the wingman was awkwardly placed for the first departure turn. SP reworked the plan before the turn point and flew the turn so the wingman held position, with no intervention by IP.
texts.3: SP chose the wingman's side from the wind, the weather and the direction of the turn out of traffic, so the wingman was on the outside of the first departure turn. The turn was flown as briefed and the assigned heading was made within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP worked out the side from the wind and the departure routing before taxi and briefed it clearly, so every turn out of traffic favored the wingman. The formation flew the whole departure with no geometry problem and rolled out on the assigned heading within 2 degrees.
texts.marginal: SP placed the wingman correctly and the departure worked, but the reasoning rested on the wind alone and the direction of the turn out of traffic was considered only at the turn point. Nothing was required from IP. SP is expected to weigh wind, weather and the turn out of traffic together when deciding which side the wingman takes.

texts_at.0: SP chose the wingman's side for the turn out of traffic with the wind and the turn direction talked through by the IP before taxi, because this is SP's first departure at this stage and weighing the wind and the turn direction together has not yet formed. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to weigh the wind and the turn direction together without the reminder on the next departures.
texts_at.1: SP placed the wingman on the wrong side for the briefed turn out of traffic, recognized only after IP pointed it out, and reached the departure heading about 10 degrees off, at the tolerance limit, before it was corrected. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to weigh the wind and the turn direction together before taxi so the side is not corrected after the error is pointed out.
texts_at.2: SP weighed the wind but not the direction of the turn out of traffic when choosing the wingman's side, then reworked the plan before the turn point and flew the turn so the wingman held position without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to weigh both factors together the first time rather than reworking the plan after choosing the side.
texts_at.3: SP chose the wingman's side from the wind and the direction of the turn out of traffic on three of the four departures, reaching the assigned heading within 5 degrees, with the fourth needing a small correction after a side choice made a beat later than ideal. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make that choice with the same promptness the first three departures showed.

texts_above.1: SP placed the wingman on the wrong side for the briefed turn and reached the departure heading to about 10 degrees off, at the tolerance limit, before the side was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP weighed the wind but not the turn direction when first choosing the wingman's side, then reworked the plan before the turn point without prompting so the wingman held position through the turn out of traffic. Weighing both factors together from the start, rather than reworking the plan afterward, would remove that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good briefing judgment for the wingman's side.
texts_above.3: SP chose the wingman's side from the wind, the weather and the direction of the turn out of traffic, so the wingman was on the outside of the first departure turn and the assigned heading was made within 5 degrees. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good briefing judgment for the wingman's side.
texts_above.4: SP worked out the wingman's side from the wind and the departure routing before taxi and briefed it clearly, so every turn out of traffic favored the wingman and the formation rolled out on the assigned heading within 2 degrees. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent briefing judgment for the wingman's side.
